extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans and researchers of British television comedy
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing the history, productions, style, and broadcast issues of the British comedy collective The Comic Strip and its TV series The Comic Strip Presents.... Useful as background for producing or studying alternative British television comedy of the 1980s–2010s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast acceptability: avoid libellous or excessively vulgar material
rubrics_metrics.description: The page notes that a planned spoof chat show script "was never produced, as it was considered too vulgar even for the 'alternative' Channel 4, and contained material that was possibly libellous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scripts intended for broadcast should be checked for potential libel and for levels of vulgarity relative to the commissioning channel's standards; material judged too vulgar or potentially libellous can lead to cancellation or non-broadcast (example: the unproduced 'Back to Normal with Eddie Monsoon').

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions for parody/adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: When parodying a copyrighted or well-known work, obtain necessary permissions: the article says 'Five Go Mad in Dorset drew anger from some viewers... although the Enid Blyton estate had given permission for the broadcast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even for satire/parody, clearance from rights-holders may be required or advisable to avoid legal disputes and public complaints; securing permission can reduce controversy (example: permission from Enid Blyton estate for parody of the Famous Five).

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode format and running time conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Early commissions were for 'six self-contained half-hour films' and most episodes ran about 30 minutes; later episodes sometimes had longer running times (around 50 minutes) and there were also feature films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan episodes according to the commissioned format (half-hour series, longer specials, or feature films). Be prepared for occasional deviations (longer episodes or theatrical release) and for different broadcasters to accept different running times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the group as actors rather than stand-up performers when producing filmed comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 commissioned 'six self-contained half-hour films... using the group as actors rather than standup performers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to present performers in character-driven film/sketch formats versus stand-up; using troupe members as actors enables narrative and spoof films rather than live stand-up recordings (example: The Comic Strip Presents... used troupe members in self-contained film episodes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic criterion: alternative/anarchic satire and parody
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic Strip is described as 'a pioneering example of the alternative comedy scene' and the series had an 'anarchic style' with heavy use of satire and parody (e.g., parodies of the Famous Five, A Fistful of Dollars, Alfred Hitchcock's Rebecca, Love Actually).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For work in this vein, prioritize anarchic tone, satirical targets, and parody conventions; expect some controversy when satirising beloved or well-known cultural properties. Use exaggerated characters, spoof formats, and inter-genre pastiche as stylistic tools (examples: 'Five Go Mad...', 'Consuela', 'Sex Actually').

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and recurring ensemble considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The troupe had core members and recurring performers; Peter Richardson is noted as the only performer to appear in every episode; later productions brought in many guest stars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a recognizable ensemble to preserve group identity, but bring in guest stars and recurring performers to broaden appeal and vary material; consider contractual attachments to signify membership (example: Richardson prompted members to sign a contract to signify their attachment to the group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning and production negotiation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The history details negotiation with a commissioning editor, budget approval, and a deal for a specific number of films (Richardson approached producer Mike Bolland; negotiated a deal with Channel 4 for six films).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching comedy projects, negotiate clear deliverables (number and length of episodes), secure budget approval from the commissioning editor, and be prepared to adapt format (e.g., films vs series) to the broadcaster's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and archive considerations for revival and distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The series moved between broadcasters (Channel 4, BBC2) and later archive episodes were broadcast on Gold; specials and one-off episodes aired sporadically over decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for multiple distribution pathways over a project's lifetime (original broadcaster, later repeats on other channels, documentary retrospectives); archival value and the ability to reunite original cast can support revivals and specials (examples: reunion specials, 30th-anniversary documentary, broadcasts on Gold).
